To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
maternal betamethsone (betaM, 100 microg.kg-1.day-1) treatment from day 15-21 in rat pregnancy causes fetal growth restriction but does not produce adult hypertension in the offspring.
betamethasome given in the last trimester of pregnancy in the lowest clinical dose does not result in hypertension or growth retardation in adult offspring.
maternal betamethsone treatment over the range from 50 to 600 microg/day/kg from day 15 of gestation to delivery in rats causes fetal growth retardatio but not adult hypertension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of glucocorticoid treatment of pregnant mothers on the development of their offspring.
the effect of maternal betamethsone on fetal and neonatal growth, and its possible effect on the development of hypertension in adult rats.
the long-term effects of antenatal betamethasome treatment on the offspring of pregnant rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fetal growth retardation caused by betamethasome treatment is dose-related, whereas hypertension is not.
betamethasones in the lowest effective dose do not cause growth retardation and hypertension in adult offspring.
betamethasones given to the rat in the last week in the lowest human equivalent dose does not produce adult hypertension, but does cause lung and placental growth retardation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetal rat is more resistant to the effects of glucocorticoids than are human neonates.
fetal lung growth is sensitive to low-dose glucocorticoid treatment, but the lowest effective doses to improve lung function are not high enough to cause hypertension in adult offspring.
the fetal lung is the most sensitive organ to the effects of antenatal corticosteroid administration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fetal growth restriction caused by maternal betamethsone is a result of a direct effect of the drug on the fetus and not a result of a reduction in uterine blood flow.
the lowest effective dose for fetal lung maturation is not associated with growth retardation and hypertension.
the lowest human clinical doses of glucocorticoids in the last week (15-21) of pregnancy in the rat do not cause hypertension or growth retardation.
